778.title: Fatimah and Ali
778.hook: the Prophet's daughter Fatimah marries Ali, and the bride price is a coat of armor (Abu Dawud)
778.howItsDone: Muslim weddings vary widely by culture, but the mahr given to the bride and a walimah, a wedding meal, are part of the practice, and some couples keep both deliberately modest, remembering Fatimah and Ali.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Badr, the day itself: two young men in the row, and a verse that called the Muslims small. Your line was: few against many.

A young man wants to marry, and he has almost nothing. That's Ali ibn Abi Talib, the Prophet's cousin. The woman is Fatimah, daughter of the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ. Ali asks for her hand, and the Prophet asks him: what will you give her? Ali says he has nothing. And the Prophet, who knows him well, asks a very practical question: where is your armor? Not a poem. Not a promise. Today: mahr.
screen: `A YOUNG MAN WITH ALMOST NOTHING.` → `WHAT WILL YOU GIVE HER?` → `WHERE IS YOUR ARMOR?`

segments.voice: The report is in the Sunan of Abu Dawud, from Ibn Abbas. Ali says he has nothing to give, the Prophet reminds him of his coat of armor, and that armor becomes the mahr, the bride's gift. In Islamic law the mahr belongs to the bride, not to her father. A report in the Sunan of an-Nasa'i lists what the Prophet gave Fatimah for the new home: a cloth, a water skin, and a leather pillow stuffed with a fragrant grass. That's the whole list. Set beside it his advice to Abd al-Rahman ibn Awf, the man from the market. In Sahih al-Bukhari, when Abd al-Rahman married, the Prophet told him to hold a wedding meal, even if only with one sheep. The meal mattered. The size didn't. Bukhari tells of a day the Prophet came to Fatimah's house and Ali wasn't there. She said there had been something between them, and he had gone out angry. The Prophet found him asleep in the mosque, his cloak slipped off, his side covered in dust, and began brushing it off him: get up, Abu Turab. Father of dust. Ali, the report says, loved that name more than any other. A small quarrel, and a father-in-law who came with a joke instead of a lecture. In Bukhari too, the Prophet says: Fatimah is a part of me. Sunni and Shi'a tradition both honor Fatimah and Ali, and this is where their household began: with very little, and with love.
screen: `THE MAHR WAS A COAT OF ARMOR.` · `A CLOTH, A WATER SKIN, A PILLOW.` · `A MEAL, EVEN WITH ONE SHEEP.` · `GET UP, ABU TURAB.` · then, large: `A SIMPLE WEDDING.`

segments.voice: Think of something coming up that you're meant to mark, a birthday, an anniversary, a small win, and notice what the plans cost, in money and in worry. Then ask what the armor is: the one thing that actually matters, a meal together, a word said out loud, the right people in the room. If you pray, you can ask Allah for blessing on the people you'll celebrate with; if not, just hold their faces in mind.
Mahr, the bride's gift. Fatimah and Ali married with a coat of armor for hers, and a home of very few things. Today's word.
Your line: a simple wedding. The gift was armor, and the home held three things. See you tomorrow.

779.title: Uhud: the archers
779.hook: the archers are told not to leave their hill, even if they see birds snatching the army; they leave for the spoils, and the victory turns (3:152; Bukhari)
779.howItsDone: Muslims read the Uhud passage of Surah Al Imran as a lesson in obedience and forgiveness, and the story of the archers is a common theme in sermons and sirah classes.

segments.voice: Yesterday, mahr: a coat of armor for a bride's gift, and a home of very few things. Your line was: a simple wedding.

Even if you see birds snatching us, don't leave this place until I send for you. That's the order, as Sahih al-Bukhari reports it, in close paraphrase. The Meccans have come back after Badr, to the foot of a mountain outside Medina called Uhud. The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ places a company of archers on a small hill, under a companion named Abdullah ibn Jubayr, to guard the army's back. The order couldn't be clearer. Whatever you see, stay. Today: Uhud.
screen: `EVEN IF YOU SEE BIRDS SNATCHING US.` → `DON'T LEAVE THIS PLACE.` → `UNTIL I SEND FOR YOU.`

segments.voice: At first, the battle goes the Muslims' way. In Bukhari's report, the Meccan line breaks and starts to run. From the hill, the archers can see it: the enemy fleeing, the camp left behind, everything there for the taking. Some start calling out: the spoils, the spoils! Your companions have won, what are you waiting for? Abdullah ibn Jubayr reminds them: have you forgotten what the Messenger of Allah told you? They answer that they'll go down to the people and take their share. And they go. The hill is left nearly empty, and the battle turns. Muslims are killed, and the Prophet himself is wounded. Surah Al Imran tells this moment without softening it. Allah kept His promise to you, the verse says, when you were driving them back, until your courage failed, and you argued about the order, and you disobeyed, after He had shown you what you longed for. Then a short line that names the whole thing, in Pickthall's words: "Some of you desired the world, and some of you desired the Hereafter." The verse doesn't name names. It says some, and some, in one army, on one afternoon. And then it does something surprising: it says Allah has forgiven them. Some Muslim teachers tell Uhud to name a very ordinary temptation: leaving your post a little early, because the reward is right there and the work looks finished.
screen: `THE MECCAN LINE BREAKS.` · `THE SPOILS, THE SPOILS!` · `HAVE YOU FORGOTTEN WHAT HE TOLD YOU?` · `THE WORLD, OR THE HEREAFTER.` · then, large: `STAY ON THE HILL.`

segments.voice: Think of one place you've been asked to hold a post, a child you're watching, a shift, a promise someone is counting on, and notice the pull toward the valley: the phone, the reward, calling it done before it is. Don't fight it; just see it clearly, the way the archers saw the spoils, and stay on the hill one breath longer. If you pray, you can ask Allah for steadiness.
Uhud: the mountain outside Medina where a victory turned, after archers left their hill for the spoils, and the verse that named it and forgave them. Today's word.
Your line: stay on the hill. The verse that named the failure also forgave it. That's day seven hundred seventy-nine.

780.title: Uhud: those who shielded him
780.hook: Nusaybah bint Ka'b, Talhah and Abu Talhah shield the wounded Prophet ﷺ with their bodies, and Fatimah tends his wound (sirah; Bukhari)
780.howItsDone: Muslims retell the defenders of Uhud in sirah lessons and sermons, and Nusaybah bint Ka'b, Umm Umarah, is named as an example of women's courage in the early community.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Uhud, and the archers who left their post for the spoils. Your line was: stay on the hill.

Same battle, a little later. The hill is empty, the enemy has come around it, and the Muslim lines have broken. People are running. The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ is hurt, and a rumor goes through the field that he has been killed. Around him, a handful of people do the opposite of running. They close in. One of them came out that morning carrying nothing but a water skin. Her name was Nusaybah bint Ka'b, and she is remembered as Umm Umarah. Today: Uhud, and the ones who stood in front.
screen: `THE LINES HAVE BROKEN.` → `A HANDFUL CLOSE IN.` → `SHE CAME OUT CARRYING WATER.`

segments.voice: Nusaybah's story comes through the early biographers, in Ibn Ishaq's account. Later, another woman asked her about Uhud, and she told it plainly. She had gone out early with a water skin, to give the fighters a drink. When the Muslims were routed, she went to where the Prophet was and fought, with a sword and with a bow, to keep people away from him, until she was wounded herself. The woman who asked saw the scar on her shoulder, deep and hollow. Nusaybah was not the only one. Sahih al-Bukhari keeps two more. A man named Qays saw the hand of Talhah ibn Ubaydullah, paralyzed: the hand he had held up to shield the Prophet at Uhud. And Anas says that Abu Talhah, a strong archer, stood before the Prophet with his shield, and when the Prophet raised his head to look at the enemy, told him: don't look out, an arrow might hit you. My chest before your chest. Then what came after. Bukhari reports that the Prophet's face was cut, his helmet broken on his head, a tooth broken. Fatimah, the bride from two days ago, washed the blood from his face while Ali poured water from his shield. When the bleeding wouldn't stop, she burned a piece of a reed mat and pressed the ash into the wound, and it stopped. A water skin, a raised hand, a shield, a handful of ash. Each of them stood between him and harm.

781.title: Medina's broken covenants
781.hook: the city's Jewish tribes and the Muslims fall into conflict, with exiles and a hard judgment on Banu Qurayza, which historians still study carefully (Bukhari; 59:2)
781.howItsDone: Muslim scholars and teachers discuss the conflicts with Medina's Jewish tribes in sirah study, through the lens of the charter and its breaking; historians of all backgrounds continue to examine the sources.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Uhud, and four people between the Prophet and harm. Your line was: she stood in front.

Some chapters are easy to tell. This one isn't, and it would be dishonest to skip it. A week ago, the charter of Medina named Jewish clans alongside the believers. That hope did not hold. One after another, three Jewish tribes of Medina came into conflict with the Muslims. Some were sent into exile. One met a judgment that is hard to read. The Muslim sources record it, and historians still study it carefully. Today, plainly: ahd.
screen: `BOUND TO DEFEND THE CITY TOGETHER.` → `THAT HOPE DID NOT HOLD.` → `TOLD AS PLAINLY AS POSSIBLE.`

segments.voice: The Muslim sources tell this as a story about covenants. The Arabic word is ahd, a pledge, a binding promise. The charter bound the groups it names to defend the city together and not to aid its enemies. The three large tribes of this story, Qaynuqa, Nadir and Qurayza, aren't named in it; Ibn Ishaq says each had its own pact with the Prophet. In his account, Qaynuqa breaks with the Muslims and leaves Medina with its goods. In Sahih al-Bukhari, Ibn Umar says Banu Nadir and Banu Qurayza fought the Muslims, and the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ sent Banu Nadir into exile and let Banu Qurayza stay. Surah al-Hashr opens on that exile: people going out from their homes, their strongholds unable to protect them. During a later siege of Medina, the sources say Banu Qurayza broke their treaty and sided with the armies outside. They surrendered and agreed to be judged by Sa'd ibn Mu'adh, a leader of the Aws, their old allies. Bukhari reports his judgment: their fighting men were to be killed, and their women and children taken captive. The Prophet accepted it. That is in the sources, and it shouldn't be smoothed over. Historians, Muslim and not, still weigh the later reports; some question details, including the numbers, which vary, and others defend them. In the Muslim sources, the judgment is framed as a sentence for breaking a treaty in wartime, not as a ruling on a people or a faith. The people of that time are not the people of this one; no one listening today, Jewish or Muslim, is on trial for it. What's asked is harder and quieter: to know it, and not to look away.
screen: `AHD: A BINDING PROMISE.` · `EXILE: QAYNUQA, THEN NADIR.` · `QURAYZA AND THE JUDGMENT OF SA'D.` · `HISTORIANS STILL WEIGH THE ACCOUNTS.` · then, large: `HARD HISTORY, TOLD HONESTLY.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind a painful chapter in a story you belong to, your country's, your faith's, and let the facts stand as they're written, without defending or attacking. When anger rises, let it pass like weather, and remember that everyone in that chapter had a face and a name. If you pray, you can ask Allah for mercy on all who suffered; if not, hold them in silence.
Ahd, a pledge. The charter, the exiles and the judgment that followed. Today's word.
Your line: hard history, told honestly. Some chapters ask only to be known. That's day seven hundred eighty-one.

782.title: The Trench
782.hook: Salman's trench, the whole city digging on a cold morning, a rock that breaks, and Jabir's small meal that feeds the diggers (Bukhari)
782.howItsDone: The Battle of the Trench, al-Khandaq, is taught in sirah classes, and the diggers' call and answer from Sahih al-Bukhari is sometimes recited as an example of the Prophet working alongside his companions.

segments.voice: Yesterday, ahd, and the hardest chapter on this stretch of the path. Your line was: hard history, told honestly.

A cold morning, and the sound of picks on stony ground. A great army of allied tribes is coming for Medina. The biographers say the plan came from Salman the Persian: dig a trench across the open side of the city. In Sahih al-Bukhari, Anas describes the Muhajirun and the Ansar, the people of Mecca and the people of Medina, digging in the cold with no servants to do it for them. The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ comes out and sees how tired and hungry they are. Today: the Trench.
screen: `A COLD MORNING.` → `SALMAN'S PLAN.` → `NO SERVANTS TO DIG FOR THEM.`

segments.voice: What he does first is sing with them. In Anas's report, he calls out a line of verse: O Allah, the real life is the life of the Hereafter, so forgive the Ansar and the Muhajirun. The diggers call back: we are the ones who pledged to Muhammad, to strive as long as we live. A call and an answer, across a ditch. Al-Bara, also in Bukhari, adds that the Prophet carried earth himself until the dust covered his belly, reciting the verses of the poet Abdullah ibn Rawahah: without You, O Allah, we would not have been guided, nor given charity, nor prayed, so send calm down on us and make our feet firm. Firm feet: the same gift as the night rain before Badr. Then the rock. Jabir says they hit a rock no one could break. The Prophet took the pick and struck, and it fell apart into loose sand. An-Nasa'i's Sunan tells of three strikes, each throwing off a flash of light. Then Jabir tells something smaller and lovelier. Seeing the Prophet's hunger, he slipped home. His wife had a little barley and a young goat; they cooked it, and Jabir quietly invited the Prophet with one or two others. Instead the Prophet called out to the whole trench: Jabir has made a meal, come on! Jabir's wife, worried, asked if the Prophet knew how little there was. He did. In Jabir's telling, everyone ate their fill, and the pot was still bubbling. Many hands, one trench, one pot.
screen: `A CALL AND AN ANSWER, ACROSS A DITCH.` · `DUST ON HIS BELLY, FEET MADE FIRM.` · `THE ROCK FALLS INTO SAND.` · `JABIR'S SMALL MEAL FOR EVERYONE.` · then, large: `DIG TOGETHER.`

segments.voice: Think of a shared job ahead, at work or after a family meal, and notice where you usually stand: in front giving directions, off to the side, or not there at all. Picture yourself in the ditch with everyone else, carrying earth, noticing who's tired and who's hungry, and what small thing you could bring, like Jabir's pot. If you pray, you can ask Allah to bless the work.
The Trench: Salman's plan, dug by the people of Mecca and Medina together in the cold, with the Prophet carrying earth and singing beside them. Today's word.
Your line: dig together. He carried the earth too, until the dust covered him. Day seven hundred eighty-two, done.

783.title: The wind
783.hook: on a freezing night of the siege, Hudhayfah crosses to the enemy camp, holds his arrow, and the wind scatters the confederate armies (33:9; Muslim)
783.howItsDone: Muslims recite the opening of the Confederates passage, 33:9 onward, as a reminder of rescue under siege, and the phrase hasbunallahu wa ni'mal wakil is said by some in hard times.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Trench: a call and an answer across a ditch, and Jabir's small pot that fed everyone. Your line was: dig together.

Who will go and bring me news of the enemy? The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ asks it of his companions on a bitter night of the siege. The trench has held, but the armies are still camped beyond it. Hudhayfah ibn al-Yaman remembers this night in Sahih Muslim. No one answers. The Prophet asks again. Silence. He asks a third time. Still no one stands up. Today: the wind.
screen: `WHO WILL BRING ME NEWS?` → `A BITTER NIGHT OF THE SIEGE.` → `NO ONE ANSWERS.`

segments.voice: Then the Prophet calls one man by name: get up, Hudhayfah. Once he was named, Hudhayfah says, he had no choice. The Prophet gives him two instructions: bring me news of them, and don't stir them up against me. So he goes, alone, across the dark. The strange part of his telling: on the way, he felt as if he were walking in a warm bath. He reaches the enemy camp and sees Abu Sufyan, the Meccan commander, warming his back at a fire. Hudhayfah fits an arrow to his bow. He says he would have hit him. Then he remembers: don't stir them up. He lowers the bow. He walks back, still warm, and gives his report, and the moment he's done, the cold comes back. The Prophet wraps him in a spare cloak he used for prayer, and Hudhayfah sleeps there until morning, when the Prophet wakes him: get up, sleeper. Meanwhile, the camp he had walked through was coming apart. Surah al-Ahzab remembers it in Pickthall's words: "O ye who believe! Remember Allah's favour unto you when there came against you hosts, and We sent against them a great wind and hosts ye could not see." The biographers say the wind knocked over pots and blew out fires, and the armies packed up and left. In Bukhari, the Prophet says afterward: now we will go to them, and they will not come to us. Notice what Hudhayfah did not do. The one dramatic act within his reach, he held back. In the Qur'an's telling, the ending came from the wind.
screen: `GET UP, HUDHAYFAH.` · `DON'T STIR THEM UP.` · `THE ARROW HELD BACK.` · `A GREAT WIND AND HOSTS YE COULD NOT SEE.` · then, large: `THE WIND CAME.`

segments.voice: Think of something you're under siege from right now, a conflict, a worry, a long wait, and notice the arrow in your hand: the angry email, the sharp word, the move that would feel good for one second and stir everything up. Hold it, the way Hudhayfah held his, and wait. If you pray, you can recite hasbunallahu wa ni'mal wakil, Allah is enough for us, and the best guardian, the words of 3:173; if not, let the storm be the storm.
The wind: the great wind of Surah al-Ahzab that broke up the armies around Medina, on the night Hudhayfah held his arrow. Today's word.
Your line: the wind came. The arrow stayed in his hand, and the ending came anyway. Until tomorrow.

784.title: The pilgrims turned back
784.hook: fourteen hundred set out as pilgrims for Mecca; the Prophet's camel kneels and won't go on, and they are stopped at the well of Hudaybiyyah (Bukhari)
784.howItsDone: Muslims setting out for hajj or umrah enter ihram at set points on the road, as the pilgrims of Hudaybiyyah did, and the story of the journey is taught in sirah classes.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the wind, and Hudhayfah lowering his bow in the enemy camp. Your line was: the wind came.

This time they aren't marching to a battle. They're going on pilgrimage. Sahih al-Bukhari describes them setting out from Medina with their sacrificial animals garlanded and marked, and entering the state of ihram, the pilgrim's state, on the road. Al-Bara, who was there, says they were fourteen hundred. The goal is the Ka'bah, the house they have faced in prayer from far away. And then, close to Mecca, the Prophet's camel kneels down in the road and won't get up. Today: the pilgrims turned back.
screen: `NOT A BATTLE: A PILGRIMAGE.` → `ANIMALS GARLANDED, PILGRIMS IN IHRAM.` → `THE CAMEL KNEELS.`

segments.voice: The camel's name is al-Qaswa, and in Bukhari's long report the people around her start saying: al-Qaswa has turned stubborn. The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ answers: she hasn't, that isn't her nature. She has been held back by the One who held back the elephant: a reference to Surah al-Fil, the army with the elephant that never reached the Ka'bah. A stopped animal, and he reads it as a sign: not this way, not by force. Then he says what sets the tone for everything after: by the One in whose hand is my soul, if they ask me for any plan that honors what Allah has made sacred, I will grant it. He turns the camel and they camp at Hudaybiyyah, at the edge of the sacred land, by a well with very little water. Al-Bara tells what happened there. They drew the well until it was dry. The Prophet sat at its edge, asked for some water, rinsed his mouth, made a supplication, and poured it back into the well. After a while, he says, the well gave enough for them and their animals. So here they are: pilgrims in ihram, water in the well, and a closed door ahead. The Meccans will not let them in. A pledge, a treaty and an argument over a single word are coming. Today is only the stopping. Much of this week has been about stopping: archers who should have stayed, defenders who held their ground, a man who held his arrow. And now a whole caravan, halted at the edge.
screen: `AL-QASWA KNEELS.` · `HELD BACK BY THE ONE WHO HELD BACK THE ELEPHANT.` · `A DRY WELL AT HUDAYBIYYAH.` · `A CLOSED DOOR AHEAD.` · then, large: `STOPPED AT THE EDGE.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one door that's closed to you right now, a job that went to someone else, a plan the world said no to, and picture yourself at its edge, ready, with your hand resting on it instead of pushing. Then turn around and look for the well: what's here, where you are, that you haven't drawn from yet. If you pray, you can ask Allah to show you the well.
Hudaybiyyah, the well at the edge of the sacred land where the pilgrim caravan, in ihram for the Ka'bah, was stopped. Today's word.
Your line: stopped at the edge. The camel knelt, and he read it as a sign. That's day seven hundred eighty-four.
